q: For clinical terminology and coding, which is the safest first analytical step?
options: Define the data grain, question and metric before joining or summarising
Immediately combine every available table
Assume similarly named fields have identical meaning
Remove records that make totals unexpected
why: The question, grain and metric definition determine correct extraction, joins and interpretation.

q: Which statement about healthcare data is correct?
options: A medication order proves the patient took the medicine
A missing code proves the condition is absent
Source, workflow and event type affect what a record means
A large dataset is automatically fit for every question
why: Healthcare records are generated by specific workflows and must be interpreted in context.

q: A rate is presented without a denominator. What is the main problem?
options: It is visually unattractive
It cannot be interpreted or reproduced reliably
It is always statistically significant
It proves data quality is poor
why: A rate requires an explicit eligible denominator, period and exclusion logic.

q: What should happen when a terminology code is mapped to another code system?
options: Discard the source code
Assume exact equivalence
Record mapping direction, version, relationship and unresolved cases
Map using display-text similarity only
why: Mappings may be broader, narrower or related rather than equivalent.

q: Which practice best protects patient information in a portfolio?
options: Use screenshots with names blurred
Upload raw hospital exports to a public repository
Use synthetic or explicitly approved de-identified data and remove secrets
Share access tokens in the README
why: Portfolio work should not expose PHI, credentials or unauthorised source data.

q: Which conclusion is most defensible from a descriptive hospital dashboard?
options: The department caused the outcome difference
The observed metric differs; case mix, completeness and workflow need review
The dashboard proves clinical effectiveness
The highest value always indicates poor care
why: Descriptive patterns identify questions for review, not causal conclusions or automatic performance judgements.
